stories.title: This Holiday Season, New York City Retail’s Split Recovery Reaches a Critical Point
stories.excerpt: The last mile is the hardest, and New York City’s retail sector is flagging near the finish line. Peter Braus, president and principal owner of Lee & Associates NYC, sees a retail market balancing two extremes. On one hand, it’s becoming increasingly hard to find the right space in the right area. One of Braus’s current clients, a “very strong” Italian brand seeking a New York City home in SoHo or along Madison Avenue, is in an especially competitive spot. The client’s preferred storefront in SoHo, for which it already had a lease out, just received a second offer. “The landlord is encouraging us to put in another offer,” Braus said. “It’s just incredibly competitive to find good space, and we’re seeing rents at levels that we haven’t seen for a really long time.” Just a few subway stops away, however, is the other end of the market spectrum, where vacancies stretch along corridors, like Broadway between City Hall and Tribeca, which Braus called “a disaster.” “I live in that area,” Braus said. “On a couple of blocks, all the stores are vacant from north to south.” New York City has nearly 142,000 storefronts, and an estimated 16,047 were vacant as of September, according to the Office of the New York City Comptroller’s recently launched vacancy dashboard. Retail vacancy citywide rose in the third quarter to 11.32 percent –– unwelcome news on the eve of the retail world’s most crucial shopping season. The citywide retail vacancy figure has hovered stubbornly between 11 percent and 11.6 percent since the third quarter of 2023, and remains above the last pre-pandemic measure of 10.5 percent. Five neighborhoods continue to see vacancies at a rate of around one in five stores, including Manhattan’s Financial District and Tribeca, Brooklyn’s Ocean Hill, and East New York and Queens’ Old Astoria-Hallets Point. bullets: NYC retail shows bifurcated recovery: prime SoHo/Madison Ave spaces ultra-competitive at record rents
Secondary corridors like Broadway (City Hall–Tribeca) face vacancy stretches described as 'disaster'
Flight-to-quality dynamic: best locations absorb demand; weaker submarkets struggle to fill space
stories.summary: New York City's retail market is splitting between tight premium corridors and distressed secondary zones. Strong international retailers compete fiercely for flagship space in SoHo and Madison Avenue at historically high rents, while nearby areas like lower Broadway show vacant storefronts. The divide reflects post-pandemic tenant consolidation toward trophy locations.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development directly, but signals broader Manhattan recovery unevenness. Flight-to-quality in retail mirrors office/residential patterns; developers should monitor which neighborhoods attract capital and foot traffic to inform mixed-use or proximate residential positioning. Weak retail corridors may suppress residential demand in adjacent areas.

stories.title: In Long Island Real Estate in 2027, Tight Supply Will Be a Key Driver
stories.excerpt: As 2027 approaches, real estate development on Long Island presents a mix of challenges and opportunities. Interest rates moved higher in 2026, and tighter lending standards have placed additional pressure on project financing. We expect financing costs to stay at or above current levels through 2027. Yet, Long island’s underlying market fundamentals remain strong, particularly in sectors where demand continues to outpace supply. Limited housing inventory and opportunities to reposition well-located aging commercial properties will continue to support investment across the region. Capital has not disappeared. Long Island investment sales reached $1.8 billion in the first half of 2026, up 21.2 percent year-over-year, according to Cushman & Wakefield. But lenders and investors will remain selective, favoring disciplined underwriting and experienced developers who understand the local market. Project selection will be critical as developers balance long-term demand against current financing costs. Scott Burman. Photo: Courtesy Burman. Housing is where we expect the most activity in 2027. Multifamily demand remains strong, supported by limited inventory, affordability challenges, and Long Island’s rapidly growing population of adults age 65 and older, underscoring the need for a broader range of housing options. Policy is beginning to help as well. 2027 will also mark the first full year under New York’s 2026 SEQRA reforms, which are designed to streamline environmental review for qualifying housing developments without overriding local zoning and permitting requirements. Another major opportunity is repositioning. According to Schuckman Realty, Long Island retail vacancy was 4.2 percent in mid-2026, asking rents were up about 9 percent year-over-year, and virtually no new retail space was being built. bullets: Long Island 2027: interest rates remain elevated; multifamily demand outpaces limited inventory
Growing 65+ population and affordability challenges drive sustained housing need on Long Island
2026 SEQRA reforms streamline environmental review; first full year of impact in 2027
stories.summary: Long Island's real estate market faces higher financing costs through 2027, but underlying multifamily fundamentals remain strong. Tight housing inventory, affordability pressures, and rapid growth of seniors age 65+ are expected to fuel demand. New York's 2026 SEQRA reforms streamline permitting for qualifying housing projects, reducing entitlement risk and timeline.
stories.impact: SEQRA reforms create a development window for Long Island multifamily projects; environmental review acceleration lowers pre-construction carry costs and risk, improving underwriting returns. Senior housing and market-rate units targeting younger households both have tailwinds. Developers should prioritize land acquisition before affordability-driven zoning changes or competing projects lock up supply.

stories.title: Mamdani Scores Critical Court Victory for Rent Freeze
stories.excerpt: Just ahead of the Thanksgiving weekend, a Manhattan Supreme Court judge sided with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani on his controversial rent freeze in a case that landlords brought against the New York City Rent Guidelines Board (RGB). The mayor called the decision “a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in.” The case stems from a 7-1 vote by the mayor-appointed RGB on June 26 halting rent increases for the city’s approximately 1 million rent-stabilized apartments. The judge in today’s ruling, Brendan T. Lantry, emphasized that his decision was not a vote for or against the wisdom of the RGB’s ruling, and that it “may cause negative collateral consequences,” but that the rent freeze was nevertheless legal. In a lawsuit filed in July, landlords had contended that the RGB ignored evidence of the rising expenses that rent-stabilized owners face in maintaining and upgrading their buildings. In some cases, the landlords said, the RGB ignored its own data, which “clearly signaled a rent increase,” according to Ann Korchak, board president of Small Property Owners of New York, whose members were plaintiffs in the lawsuit. “This ruling is terribly disappointing to small property owners,” Korchak said in a statement on Wednesday. “The rent freeze will push more small rent-stabilized property owners to the edge of the cliff. It denies the resources they need to maintain and operate their rent-stabilized buildings. Property taxes, water and sewer rates, and insurance, energy, heating, repair and other costs and expenses aren’t frozen. Rents should not be frozen, either.” Randy Mastro, a lawyer for the landlords in the case, said in a statement to Commercial Observer that they were “disappointed by the court’s ruling.” “The judge acknowledged multiple irregularities in the RGB’s process and, in particular, called out Mayor Mamdani’s ‘comments, promises and guarant
bullets: NYC court upholds Mayor Mamdani's 7-1 Rent Guidelines Board vote freezing ~1M rent-stabilized apartments
Judge acknowledged ruling 'may cause negative collateral consequences' but found freeze legal
Landlords' argument that rising expenses justify increases rejected; regulatory risk now entrenched
stories.summary: A Manhattan Supreme Court judge upheld New York's controversial rent freeze on approximately 1 million rent-stabilized apartments, validating a June 2026 RGB vote halting increases. Though the judge acknowledged potential negative fallout, he found the freeze legally sound despite landlord arguments about rising maintenance and upgrade costs. The ruling eliminates immediate legal challenge to the policy.
stories.impact: SEVERE IMPACT: NYC rent-stabilized portfolio owners face zero rent-increase revenue for the foreseeable future, creating massive cash flow pressure and refinancing risk on rent-stabilized properties. This deepens incentives for new development (all-market-rate) and conversion/repositioning of non-stabilized stock. Market-rate multifamily demand and NOI growth in NYC will accelerate as RS properties struggle and capital flees; stabilized building sales may spike at distressed prices, creating acquisition opportunities for buyers accepting permanent rent caps.

stories.title: Netflix Acquiring Historic Radford Studio Center for $380M
stories.excerpt: Netflix has reached an agreement to acquire the historic Radford Studio Center in Studio City for a reported $380 million, marking the streaming giant’s first purchase of a Los Angeles-area studio lot. The property is located at 4024 Radford Avenue, just off Ventura Blvd in the southeastern San Fernando Valley, close to Hollywood, Burbank and many other entertainment-related businesses. As reported by the L.A. Times and other sources, Goldman Sachs took control of the property in January after its previous owner, Hackman Capital Partners, defaulted on a $1.1 billion mortgage amid a slowdown in Hollywood production. Hackman and Square Mile Capital Management acquired the property for $1.85 billion in 2021. The 1.14 million-square-foot production campus features 22 soundstages, 18 office buildings and 20 bungalows. Founded in 1928 by filmmaker Mack Sennett, the studio has been home to numerous iconic television series, including Seinfeld, Gilligan’s Island, Will & Grace and The Mary Tyler Moore Show. The acquisition represents a significant expansion of Netflix’s Southern California real estate holdings. The company currently leases approximately 2 million square feet of office and soundstage space in Los Angeles. Netflix intends to retain Radford’s existing studio team and maintain operations at the production campus. bullets: Netflix acquires Radford Studio Center, Studio City, for $380M; first LA studio lot purchase
Goldman Sachs foreclosed after owner Hackman defaulted on $1.1B debt amid production slowdown

stories.summary: Netflix bought the historic Radford Studio Center in Studio City for $380 million, its first acquisition of an LA-area studio lot. Goldman Sachs had taken control after Hackman Capital Partners' default on a $1.1 billion mortgage in early 2026. The deal expands Netflix's production footprint; the company currently leases approximately 2 million square feet of LA office and soundstage space.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact. However, Netflix's ownership consolidation and shift from lease to ownership signals optimism in LA media/entertainment production recovery post-slowdown. This may stabilize or strengthen employment and population in Studio City, Burbank, and San Fernando Valley submarkets, providing longer-term residential demand tailwinds for multifamily developers in those corridors—especially if Netflix ramps content production and hiring.

stories.title: Fairstead Closes $17M Affordable Housing Transaction in Oklahoma
stories.excerpt: Fairstead announced its $16.5 million acquisition of London Square Village Apartments, a 200-unit project-based Section 8 community in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, and plans for a comprehensive rehabilitation of the property. The transaction marks Fairstead’s first acquisition in Oklahoma. London Square Village Apartments consists of 200 units across 18 two-story residential buildings and a community center. The community includes 24 one-bedroom, 96 two-bedroom and 80 three-bedroom homes, with all units reserved for households earning at or below 60% of the area median income.  “Expanding into Oklahoma represents an important step in Fairstead’s mission to preserve sustainable, reliable affordable housing for communities across the country,” said Jeff Goldberg, Founder and CEO of Fairstead. The acquisition will preserve London Square Village Apartments as affordable housing through 4% federal LIHTC equity from R4 Capital and tax-exempt bond financing issued by the Oklahoma Housing Finance Agency, with R4 Capital also serving as lender. Join us for the Connect Midwest Multifamily conference on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 8, 2027, at Joe’s Live in Rosemont, Illinois. stories.summary: Fairstead closed its first Oklahoma acquisition: London Square Village Apartments, a 200-unit project-based Section 8 community in Oklahoma City, for $16.5 million. The deal is financed through 4% LIHTC equity and tax-exempt bonds from the Oklahoma Housing Finance Agency. The property will undergo comprehensive rehabilitation and remain affordable.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to market-rate multifamily development. Signals institutional capital's continued confidence in affordable/subsidized housing preservation (LIHTC, PBV). For-profit developers should note Fairstead's market entry into Oklahoma; suggests investor appetite for underserved metros. If Fairstead's success attracts additional LIHTC-focused capital to Oklahoma, it may tighten public financing availability for market-rate projects competing for state/local resources.

stories.title: Dwight Capital Finances $52M Loan for Mixed-Use Multifamily Community in Michigan
stories.excerpt: Dwight Capital has closed a $52 million HUD 223(f) loan for Griffin Royal Oak, a 245-unit luxury mixed-use multifamily community in the heart of Royal Oak, Michigan. Developed by Singh Development, the property features a five-story residential building, an attached parking garage, and four ground-floor commercial spaces totaling 9,000 square feet. Strategically located near downtown Royal Oak, Griffin Royal Oak is surrounded by pedestrian-friendly sidewalks, boutiques, salons, and retail shops, and more than 70 restaurants. The property’s luxury residences, ground-floor retail, and walkable location reflect Singh Development’s focus on thoughtfully designed communities in desirable locations. “Griffin Royal Oak represents the type of community we have focused on developing for more than five decades—high-quality residential environments in strong, established markets,” said Saab Grewal of Singh Development. Dwight Capital’s Karnveer Bal and Alex Shoenfeld originated the loan on behalf of Singh Development, an established, family-owned real estate development and investment company. stories.title: Host Hotels Rounds Out $202M Brooklyn Hotel Buy With $29M Retail, Parking Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Host Hotels & Resorts has secured three retail spaces and an indoor parking area at its newly acquired hotel asset in Brooklyn’s Dumbo neighborhood. The Bethesda, Md.-based real estate investment trust, through the entity Brooklyn Bridge Hotel Owner, acquired the commercial condo units and parking space at 90 Furman Street from a Starwood Capital Group entity, according to property records filed Wednesday. All four properties were built in 2015, according to city tax records, and adjoin Host Hotel’s newest portfolio addition, 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge at 60 Furman Street. Host Hotel acquired the hotel’s 85-year leasehold interest from Starwood in a $202 million all-cash deal announced earlier this month. The 195-key hotel marks a significant feather in Host Hotel’s cap, as the operator expects 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge to be among its top 10 assets based on full-year estimates. A second agreement, this one concerning the takeover and restructuring of an existing $113 million debt on the properties at 90 Furman and 60 Furman Street, was also filed in city records Wednesday. The properties’ existing mortgage was previously held by Sumitomo Mitsui Banking, according to the filing, and has now been assigned to the entity TRS NY Lender. The same entity has previously been linked by The Real Deal to the New York State Teachers’ Retirement System of NYC, which financed Host Hotels’ 2024 purchase of Starwood’s 1 Hotel Central Park at 1414 Avenue of the Americas. That $265 million deal was in one of that year’s top 10 investment sales. Host Hotels’ recent acquisition of the Dumbo hotel came on the heels of a $127 million all-cash purchase of the 308-room Renaissance Dallas at Plano Legacy West Hotel in Texas. The seller was a joint venture of Paceline Equity Partners and Aravest. Spokespeople for Host Hotels and Starwood did not respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Host Hotels acquires 85-year leasehold at 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge (195 keys) for $202M all-cash
Adds $29M for adjacent retail spaces and parking; asset expected top-10 performing in portfolio

stories.summary: Host Hotels closed a $202 million all-cash acquisition of a 195-key hotel leasehold at 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge in Brooklyn's Dumbo neighborhood, plus a $29 million add-on for three retail spaces and parking. The company expects the hotel to rank in its top 10 performing assets. Host also refinanced $113 million in existing debt on the combined portfolio.
stories.impact: Moderate relevance. Host's confident capital deployment in Dumbo (all-cash, top-10 asset designation) signals sustained demand for high-end hospitality in Brooklyn waterfront submarkets. This capital intensity and pricing power suggest strong visitor traffic and local spending, supporting retail and restaurant ecosystems. Nearby multifamily (especially luxury, mixed-use) will benefit from halo effect. However, $202M all-cash spend indicates tight capital environment; multifamily developers may face stiffer competition for debt/equity in Dumbo submarkets.

stories.title: Thor Equities Buys San Francisco Office/Retail Asset for $50.5M, Lands $51.8M Loan
stories.excerpt: Thor Equities has acquired 55 Stockton Street, a boutique Class A office and retail property in San Francisco’s Union Square district, from Zaber Corporation for $50.5 million. The company also secured $51.8 million in acquisition financing from Prime Finance. Also known as the National Center Building, the eight-story, 136,714-square-foot property is situated at the corner of Stockton and O’Farrell streets, one block south of Union Square. Built in 1988 and renovated in 2023, the building features three floors of retail space with boutique office space above. Office tenants include Chalk AI, Harness and Taylor & Associates Architects. The acquisition expands Thor’s presence in the Union Square district. The firm acquired nearby 146 Geary St., home to Bang & Olufsen’s flagship store, for $20.5 million in August. Thor also owns 152 Geary St., occupied by Banana Republic. The property offers convenient access to public transportation and is surrounded by prominent retail, dining and hospitality destinations. Newmark’s Chris Kramer, Ricky Braha, Tim Polglase and Dante DiStefano arranged the financing on behalf of Thor Equities. The 136,714-square-foot building, recently renovated in 2023, features three floors of retail and boutique office space. The deal bolsters Thor's presence in Union Square.

Developers should monitor Union Square's retail/office absorption; if sustained, it supports case for luxury multifamily infill or conversion plays nearby.

stories.title: OC Investor Group Buys Two Apartment Properties in Venice
stories.excerpt: A group of private Orange County-based investors acquired two multifamily properties totaling 40 units in the coastal Los Angeles community of Venice for $14.23 million. The properties, located at 1400 and 1500 Venice Blvd., were sold by Advanced Real Estate Group. The transaction, which partly included 1031 exchange capital, worked out to $355,662 per unit and $430 per square foot. Colliers’ Kitty Wallace represented the seller and, along with colleague Andy Eberhard, also represented the buyers. Built in 1988 and 1985, respectively, the properties encompass 33,072 square feet of building area and offer 77 parking spaces. Neither property is subject to the City of Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance. The 31-unit property at 1400 Venice Blvd. features renovated interiors, a fitness center, a rooftop lounge and subterranean parking. The nine-unit property at 1500 Venice Blvd. sold above its asking price for approximately $3.43 million, representing a 5.13% capitalization rate. The new ownership plans to continue the previous ownership’s unit renovation program. Photo is of 1500 Venice Blvd. The post OC Investor Group Buys Two Apartment Properties in Venice appeared first on Connect CRE.

The 31-unit property at 1400 Venice Boulevard features amenities; the nine-unit at 1500 Venice Boulevard sold above asking price at a 5.13% cap rate. Non-RSO status makes Venice portfolio attractive to yield-focused buyers and developers. The 1031 exchange capital deployment signals outflows from other CA markets. Developers should monitor Venice/coastal LA multifamily pricing; if caps remain compressed and rents continue rising, acquisition windows may close for new development—prioritize land control and entitlements in Venice, Santa Monica, Manhattan Beach submarkets.

stories.title: Flight to Quality Deepens Divide Among Major U.S. Office Markets
stories.excerpt: The U.S. office market is showing more signs of improvement, but the recovery remains uneven across the nation’s biggest cities. The national office vacancy rate declined 140 basis points annually to 17.2 percent in October, while average asking rents increased 1.5 percent to $33.30 per square foot, according to a report using Yardi data. Office sales totaled nearly $56.9 billion across 2,576 transactions through the first 10 months of 2026, with properties trading at an average of $197 per square foot. But the flight to quality is widening the performance gap between newer and older properties, the report found. Asking rents for Class A office space increased 2.5 percent over the past year, while rents for Class B space declined 0.3 percent. “Office employment growth doesn’t always translate into an office market rebound, and we are seeing significant market discrepancies,” Peter Kolaczynski, director of Yardi Research, said in the report. “One consistency, though, is that outdated and less amenitized buildings are facing the most pressure, while new deliveries are offering best-in-class product and obtaining rent premiums.” Manhattan led the nation’s largest office markets in investment volume, construction activity, asking rents and occupancy in October. Investors traded more than $6.2 billion worth of Manhattan office properties in the first 10 months of the year at an average of $533 per square foot. Meanwhile, Manhattan’s average asking rents increased 9.5 percent annually to $74.44 per square foot, more than double the national average. The borough also had 3.73 million square feet of office space under construction, the largest development pipeline in the country. Miami recorded the strongest annual office rent growth among the markets tracked, with asking rates jumping 12.8 percent to $63.58 per square foot. The South Florida market’s office-using employment increased 22.1 percent since January 2021, while its office inventory expanded just 5.3 percen
bullets: US office vacancy declined 140 bps YoY to 17.2%; asking rents +1.5% to $33.30/sf through Oct 2026
Class A rents +2.5% YoY; Class B rents -0.3%; flight-to-quality widens gap; 2,576 sales, $56.9B YTD
Outdated, less amenitized buildings face most pressure; new, Class A stock commands rent growth
stories.summary: The U.S. office market improved in 2026 with vacancy down 140 basis points to 17.2% and asking rents up 1.5% to $33.30 per square foot. However, the recovery is uneven: Class A rents rose 2.5% year-over-year while Class B fell 0.3%. The flight-to-quality dynamic is widening the performance gap between newer, well-amenitized buildings and older, outdated stock. Office sales totaled $56.9 billion across 2,576 transactions through October.
stories.impact: Office market bifurcation mirrors residential: Class A, urban-core, mixed-use properties benefit; aging, suburban, non-amenitized buildings suffer. This suggests multifamily developers should prioritize new-construction or heavily renovated, Class A, mixed-use projects in urban cores or strong suburban nodes. Flight-to-quality capital and tenant preferences are intact; dated multifamily stock will underperform. Conversion of distressed office to multifamily may accelerate in secondary markets; acquisition prices for obsolete office will compress, improving conversion economics in soft office markets like Austin, Denver.
